_link.title: I can describe how an electron gun accelerates electrons and calculate the speed of electrons using qV = ½mv²

toLevel2.stem: In an electron gun, what is heated to release electrons?
distractors: The anode
The magnet
The filament shield

toLevel2.stem: Which formula relates the accelerating voltage to the kinetic energy gained by an electron?
distractors: F = qvB
E = mc²
V = IR

toLevel2.stem: What does the voltage V represent in the equation qV = ½mv²?
distractors: The speed of the electron beam
The magnetic field strength value
The resistance of the cathode wire

toLevel2.stem: What energy conversion occurs when an electron is accelerated through a potential difference in an electron gun?
toLevel2.answer: Electric potential energy converts to kinetic energy
distractors: Kinetic energy converts to thermal energy output
Magnetic energy converts to electric potential energy
Gravitational energy converts to kinetic energy

toLevel2.stem: What is the rearranged formula to calculate the speed of an electron accelerated from rest?
distractors: v = qV/(2m)
v = 2qV/m
v = √(qV/2m)

toLevel2.stem: An electron gun heats a {{blank:1}} to release electrons, which are then accelerated toward an {{blank:2}}.
The work done on the electron by the electric field equals {{blank:1}}, which converts to {{blank:2}} energy.
The speed of an accelerated electron is found using v = √(2{{blank:1}}/{{blank:2}}).
In an electron gun, electrons are accelerated by a magnetic field.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: The kinetic energy gained by an electron in an electron gun equals the charge multiplied by the accelerating voltage.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Why does the equation qV = ½mv² assume the electron starts from rest?
toLevel3.answer: If the electron starts from rest, all the energy from the voltage converts to kinetic energy with no initial kinetic energy to add
distractors: Electrons released from a heated cathode always have exactly zero thermal energy initially
The equation only works for particles at rest because moving particles cannot gain energy
The voltage cannot accelerate a particle that is already moving through the electric field

toLevel3.stem: An electron is accelerated through 500 V. What kinetic energy does it gain?
Why is an electric field used to accelerate electrons rather than a magnetic field?
toLevel3.answer: Electric fields can do work on charges and increase their speed; magnetic fields cannot
distractors: Magnetic fields are too weak to exert any force on electrons at all inside the gun
Electric fields are cheaper to produce than magnetic fields in laboratory settings
Magnetic fields would cause the electrons to lose energy through radiation losses

toLevel3.stem: If the accelerating voltage is doubled, by what factor does the electron's speed increase?
distractors: By a factor of 2
By a factor of 4
By a factor of ½

toLevel3.stem: What does the equation qV = ½mv² tell us about the relationship between voltage and kinetic energy?
toLevel3.answer: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to the accelerating voltage
distractors: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the accelerating voltage
Kinetic energy is inversely proportional to the accelerating voltage value
Kinetic energy is independent of the accelerating voltage applied

toLevel3.stem: An electron accelerated through 1000 V reaches approximately 1.87 × 10⁷ m/s. Why is this much faster than everyday objects?
toLevel3.answer: The electron's extremely small mass means even a small energy input produces a very high speed
distractors: The electric field is much stronger than any force that acts on everyday macroscopic objects
Electrons can exceed the normal speed limits that apply to objects with visible mass only
The voltage of 1000 V provides an unusually large amount of energy compared to other forces

toLevel3.stem: Doubling the voltage {{blank:1}} the kinetic energy and increases the speed by a factor of {{blank:2}}.
The electron gun uses an {{blank:1}} field to accelerate electrons, not a {{blank:2}} field.
An electron accelerated through 500 V gains kinetic energy of {{blank:1}} × 10⁻¹⁷ J, because Ek = {{blank:2}}.
Doubling the accelerating voltage doubles the speed of the electron.
distractors: True

toLevel4.stem: Calculate the speed of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2000 V. (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
An electron exits an electron gun with speed 1.0 × 10⁷ m/s. What accelerating voltage was used?
A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is accelerated through the same voltage as an electron. How does its final speed compare to the electron's?
toLevel4.answer: The proton is much slower because its mass is much larger
distractors: The proton has the same speed because both have the same charge
The proton is faster because it has a greater charge-to-mass ratio
The proton is faster because heavier particles gain more kinetic energy

toLevel4.stem: An electron is accelerated through 5000 V. Calculate its kinetic energy and speed.
An electron gun produces electrons with 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ J of kinetic energy. What voltage was applied?
In a cathode ray tube, electrons are accelerated through 20 kV. At this speed (about 0.28c), should relativistic effects be considered?
toLevel4.answer: At 0.28c relativistic effects are noticeable but small; for high precision they should be considered
distractors: At 0.28c the classical formula is perfectly accurate with zero error in the calculation
Relativistic effects only matter above 0.99c so they are completely irrelevant at 0.28c
At any speed above 0.01c the classical formula is entirely useless and cannot be applied

toLevel4.stem: Two electron guns use 500 V and 2000 V respectively. What is the ratio of the electron speeds (v₅₀₀ : v₂₀₀₀)?
An electron accelerated through 3000 V gains kinetic energy of {{blank:1}} × 10⁻¹⁶ J and reaches a speed of approximately {{blank:2}} × 10⁷ m/s.
To find the voltage from a known speed, rearrange to V = {{blank:1}} / ({{blank:2}}).
The speed ratio of electrons from two guns is proportional to the {{blank:1}} root of the {{blank:2}} ratio.

toLevel5.stem: A student uses qV = ½mv² to calculate the speed of an electron accelerated through 500 kV and gets v = 4.2 × 10⁸ m/s, which exceeds the speed of light. Evaluate this result.
toLevel5.answer: The classical formula breaks down at high energies; relativistic mechanics must be used, which limits the speed to below c
distractors: The calculation is correct; electrons can exceed the speed of light when given enough energy
The error is in the mass value used; at high speeds the mass is zero so the formula fails
The formula is wrong because it should be qV = mv² without the factor of one-half included

toLevel5.stem: Compare the electron gun in a cathode ray tube with the electron source in a synchrotron. How do their roles differ?
toLevel5.answer: Both produce initial electrons, but the synchrotron uses additional stages of acceleration to reach much higher energies
distractors: The cathode ray tube accelerates electrons to higher speeds than any synchrotron can achieve
The synchrotron does not use an electron source; it creates electrons from magnetic energy
Both produce electrons at the same final speed; only the path shapes differ between them

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why electrons reach much higher speeds than protons when accelerated through the same voltage.
toLevel5.answer: Both gain the same kinetic energy (qV), but the electron's much smaller mass means v = √(2qV/m) gives a much larger speed
distractors: Electrons gain more kinetic energy because they have a higher charge than protons have
Protons experience more friction from the electric field which limits their maximum speed
The voltage pushes electrons harder than protons because electrons are negatively charged

toLevel5.stem: In an electron microscope, resolution improves with higher electron speed. Using qV = ½mv², explain how voltage affects resolution.
toLevel5.answer: Higher voltage increases electron speed, which decreases their de Broglie wavelength and improves resolution
distractors: Higher voltage makes electrons brighter so the microscope can see finer details in images
Higher voltage increases the electron's charge giving it more ability to interact with samples
Higher voltage has no effect on resolution; only the magnetic lens strength matters here

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that using a negative anode would accelerate electrons even faster. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; a negative anode would repel electrons, preventing acceleration toward it entirely
distractors: Correct; a negative anode provides twice the acceleration by pulling and pushing simultaneously
Correct; the sign of the anode does not matter because electrons will always be accelerated
Incorrect; but only because negative voltages cannot exist in laboratory equipment systems

toLevel5.stem: Compare the energy efficiency of an electron gun to a linear accelerator. Which analysis is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Both convert electrical potential energy to kinetic energy; the efficiency depends on losses such as heating and radiation
distractors: Electron guns are perfectly 100% efficient because all voltage converts to kinetic energy
Linear accelerators are always more efficient because they use magnetic fields for acceleration
Both are equally efficient because they both use the same equation qV = ½mv² for operation

toLevel5.stem: An electron gun operates at 10 kV. Calculate the electron's speed and assess whether relativistic corrections are needed.
toLevel5.answer: v ≈ 5.9 × 10⁷ m/s (about 0.20c); relativistic effects are small but present, classical formula is a reasonable approximation
distractors: v ≈ 5.9 × 10⁸ m/s (about 2.0c); relativistic corrections are essential at this speed value
v ≈ 5.9 × 10⁶ m/s (about 0.02c); relativistic effects are completely negligible at this speed
v ≈ 5.9 × 10⁷ m/s (about 0.20c); the classical formula is perfectly accurate up to 0.5c

toLevel5.stem: Explain why the electron gun uses thermionic emission rather than simply placing electrons in the electric field.
toLevel5.answer: Electrons must be freed from the metal surface first; thermionic emission provides free electrons that the field can then accelerate
distractors: The electric field alone would produce too many electrons causing the beam to be unstable
Thermionic emission creates faster electrons than the electric field could produce by itself
The electric field cannot interact with electrons unless they have first been thermally heated

toLevel5.stem: At very high voltages the classical formula predicts speeds exceeding {{blank:1}}, indicating that {{blank:2}} mechanics must be used instead.
Thermionic emission frees electrons from the {{blank:1}} by heating it, providing the free charges that the {{blank:2}} field then accelerates.
